--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [offices()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} | EdgeCase description: The rooms of a two-story office and the doors between them. twitter-card: title: >- [offices()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} | EdgeCase description: The rooms of a two-story office and the doors between them. title: >- [offices()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: The rooms of a two-story office and the doors between them. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} The rooms of a two-story office and the doors between them. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/example_networks.py#L1467-L1542){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature offices() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The floor plan of a made-up office, as a graph of its 20 rooms, joined where a door leads from one to the other, and the staircase between the two floors. It's the example for covering problems on a building: the fewest rooms from which every room can be watched (a dominating set), the most rooms with no door between any two (an independent set), and coloring the rooms so no two next to each other match. Every room has a position on the plan, so `plot(layout="pos")` draws the two floors, one above the other. Network Properties: - 20 nodes (rooms, labeled by name) - 23 edges (22 doors and the staircase) - Undirected, unweighted - Connected and planar Node Attributes: - `floor`: `1` or `2` - `kind`: `"common"` (lobby, reception, kitchen, library and lounge), `"hall"`, `"stairs"`, `"meeting"`, `"office"` or `"server"` - `pos`: the room's `(x, y)` position on the plan, in meters, with the second floor drawn above the first Edge Attributes: - `kind`: `"door"`, or `"stairs"` for the staircase What to Look For: - **Four halls watch every room.** Every room is one of the four halls or has a door into one, and no three rooms manage that, so the halls are the smallest dominating set, and the only one of that size. `minimum_weighted_dominating_set()` finds them, while the quicker `dominating_set()` returns a dominating set of 10 rooms. - **One way between floors.** The staircase is the only connection between the floors, so it's a bridge, and both stairwells are articulation points. So are the four halls, since some rooms open onto nothing else. - **Three colors.** The Lobby, Reception and West Hall 1 all open onto each other, so coloring the rooms takes at least 3 colors, and DSATUR manages with 3. - **Eleven rooms with no door between them.** The largest independent set has 11 of the 20 rooms. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The floor plan. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Draw the plan, colored by the kind of room: ::: {#0dba0f1e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec offices = ec.offices() offices.plot(layout="pos", color_by="kind", label_by="label") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Every room is one of the four halls, or next to one: ::: {#f8424e8d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} halls = offices.minimum_weighted_dominating_set() offices.plot(layout="pos", highlight=halls, label_by="label") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
